book:web_a7298a6c.description: Travelogue and ethnographic study of Central Asia by American diplomat and scholar Eugene Schuyler, first published in 1876.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a specific volume and page of Schuyler's work on Turkistan.

book:web_98299447.description: A collection and study of Russian folk songs, published in 1872 by the British scholar William Ralston Shedden-Ralston.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Ralston's work on Russian folk songs.
James George Frazer cites Ralston's work on Russian songs.

book:web_9d42a10c.description: A detailed ethnographic and geographical account of the Cape of Good Hope, originally written in German as 'Caput Bonae Spei Hodiernum' (1719) and translated into English in 1731.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Kolben's book as a source.

book:web_571ea72a.description: A book by James Africanus Horton, a Sierra Leonean writer and surgeon, published in London in 1868, discussing the peoples and countries of West Africa.
commentaries: James George Frazer notes that Horton's book repeats information from another source.

book:web_84cf8a9d.description: A foundational work on Greek etymology by the German philologist Georg Curtius, first published in 1858 and subsequently revised in multiple editions.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Curtius's work on Greek etymology for the derivation of the names Zeus and Jove.

book:web_7d7e17fe.description: A report on the island of Nias (Indonesia) by Dutch colonial officials/ethnographers, published in the 19th century.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a book by Nieuwenhuisen and Rosenberg about the island of Nias.

book:web_9e2309ca.description: A two-volume travelogue describing the author's experiences in southeastern Africa, including observations on Zulu customs such as the first-fruits festival.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Isaacs' travel book as a source for the Zulu feast of first-fruits.
James George Frazer cites Adair's history as a source describing a ceremony.
James George Frazer cites Adair's history of American Indians twice: once regarding warriors not sitting on the ground, and once for the sacred ark.

book:web_89aec46d.description: A detailed study of Roman religious institutions and sacred law, forming the second volume of Marquardt's comprehensive work on Roman state administration.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Marquardt's work to support the timing of the Salii processions.

book:web_532a2157.description: An ethnographic work on New Guinea and its inhabitants by the German ethnographer and naturalist Otto Finsch.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Otto Finsch’s book on New Guinea and its inhabitants.

book:web_5999f06e.description: A two-volume work on German folk beliefs and customs, examining their roots in pre-Christian antiquity.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Rochholz's work on German belief and custom.

book:web_4e407cd1.description: A collection of early Latin fragments and specimens, compiled by the classical scholar John Wordsworth.
commentaries: James George Frazer refers to Wordsworth's collection for a textual emendation.

book:8315520.description:
The "Saturnalia," Macrobius's encyclopedic celebration of Roman culture written in the early fifth century CE, has been prized since the Renaissance as a treasure trove of otherwise unattested lore. Cast in the form of a dialogue, the "Saturnalia" treats subjects as diverse as the divinity of the Sun and the quirks of human digestion while showcasing Virgil as the master of all human knowledge from diction and rhetoric to philosophy and religion.
The new Latin text is based on a refined understanding of the...
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Macrobius' Saturnalia for a reference.
James George Frazer cites Macrobius's work on the mother of the Lares.
James George Frazer cites Macrobius's Saturnalia as evidence for the Matronalia feast.
Pliny the Elder mentions Macrobius as a source for the Fescennine verses written by Augustus.
Pliny the Elder cites Macrobius's 'Saturnalia' as a source for the story of Cleopatra dissolving pearls in vinegar.

book:web_ece55bd4.description: A detailed ethnographic account of Chinese customs and society in the mid-19th century, based on the author's experiences as a missionary in Fuzhou.
commentaries: James George Frazer references Doolittle's book for a detail about Chinese social life.

book:web_2db7b22c.description: A multi-volume work on the indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast of North America, originally published in five volumes between 1875 and 1876.
commentaries: James George Frazer references Bancroft's book as a source for details about Mexican customs.
James George Frazer cites Bancroft's work on Native American races.
James George Frazer cites Bancroft's work as a source for Mexican instances of persons representing deities.
James George Frazer cites Bancroft’s work on native races.

book:web_04ec60c2.description: A collection of German legends and folk tales by Ludwig Bechstein, first published in 1853.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Bechstein's collections of German and Thuringian legends.

book:web_5ea19f76.description: A detailed account of Burmese life and customs by a British colonial administrator, originally published under the pseudonym Shway Yoe.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites volumes and pages of Shway Yoe's work on the Burmans.

book:web_6372f96d.description: A historical and descriptive account of British Burma, likely by Charles James Forbes (or possibly Forbes, a colonial administrator), published in the late 19th century.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a page from Forbes's book on British Burma.

book:web_813f9d59.description: A two-volume work on the Batak lands of Sumatra by the naturalist and explorer Franz Junghuhn, published in the mid-19th century.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Junghuhn's book on the Batak lands in Sumatra.

book:web_2935779d.description: A historical and descriptive account of Queensland, Australia, by John Dunmore Lang, first published in 1861. The citation refers to a contribution by the Rev. W. Ridley within this work.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a contribution by Ridley within Lang's book on Queensland.

book:web_219b1b4f.description: A collection of folklore from Shropshire, England, co-authored by Charlotte Sophia Burne and Georgina F. Jackson.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Burne and Jackson's collection of Shropshire folklore.

book:web_1176e22c.description: A study by the German classical philologist and mythographer Wilhelm Heinrich Roscher, comparing the Greek god Apollo with the Roman god Mars.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Roscher's work Apollon und Mars in the context of discussions about the name Veturius.

book:web_8ef97992.description: A scholarly work on Lithuanian linguistics and folklore by the German philologist Adalbert Bezzenberger, published in Göttingen in 1882.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Bezzenberger's book as a source for information about Lithuanian research.

book:web_ee318117.description: An ethnographic work on the tribes of the Hindu Kush region, first published in 1880 by Colonel John Biddulph.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Biddulph's book as a source of information about tribes of the Hindoo Koosh.

book:web_05c1b17f.description: A collection of fairy tales and legends from the Italian-speaking part of Tyrol (Wälschtirol), compiled and published by Christian Schneller.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Schneller's collection of tales from Welschtirol.

book:web_f19a04a4.description: A study of the Kamilaroi Aboriginal people of Australia, including their language and customs, by missionary and linguist William Ridley.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites this book as a source for a specific fact or observation.
James George Frazer cites Ridley's book on the Kamilaroi people.

book:web_e89701f8.description: A historical geography book detailing the Russian expansion along the Amur River and the colonization of the region.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Ravenstein's book as a source for the location of a group of people.

book:web_f855326e.description: A multi-volume history of antiquity by the German historian Eduard Meyer, first published in 1884.
commentaries: James George Frazer references this historical work.

book:2027513.description: Longtemps considere comme naif ou maladroit, Le grand voyage du pays des Hurons apparait aujourd'hui comme un document ethnographique exceptionnel. Compte rendu d'une enquete de dix mois sur le terrain en 1623-1624, au moment ou les Hurons n'avaient pas encore subi l'influence de la culture europeenne, ce voyage se revele aussi comme texte litteraire, porte par un narrateur curieux, emerveille, et qui sait utiliser toutes les ressources de la rhetorique pour captiver son lecteur.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Sagard's book about the Huron country.

book:web_644deefe.description: A 9th-century Byzantine work by Photius, summarizing and reviewing numerous ancient Greek texts, often cited by manuscript page numbers from Bekker's edition.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Helladius as preserved in Photius's Bibliotheca.

book:web_61f79f2a.description: A work on Roman festivals and the calendar by the 6th-century Byzantine writer Joannes Lydus.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Joannes Lydus on the Matronalia.
James George Frazer cites Lydus's work on months for information on the Ides of March expulsion.

book:web_4273e64b.description: A multi-volume anthropological study of indigenous peoples, first published in 1859.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Waitz's work as a source.

book:web_458e7a71.description: A study of German sacrificial customs, frequently cited in James Frazer's The Golden Bough.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Jahn's work on German sacrificial customs as a source.

book:web_a0bfe39e.description: A two-volume work on Japan by German geographer Johannes Justus Rein, first published in 1881 (vol. 1) and 1886 (vol. 2). The citation refers to volume 1, page 447.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Rein's book as a source.

book:web_fa2c08d4.description: A collection of Greek and Roman myths, often cited as 'Fabularum' in Latin, by the Roman author Gaius Julius Hyginus.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Hyginus' Fables.

book:web_897ebb05.description: A scholarly work on Gnosticism and related artifacts by the British antiquarian and gem collector C. W. King, first published in 1887.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites King's work on the Gnostics.

book:web_0135101e.description: A comprehensive study of German folk superstitions, first published in 1860 by theologian and folklorist Adolf Wuttke.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Wuttke's work on German popular superstitions.
James George Frazer cites Wuttke's book on German folk superstitions.

book:web_a78f6d81.description: An account of three years among the cannibals of New Britain, related to the custom in New Ireland mentioned in The Golden Bough.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Powell’s account of the New Ireland custom as a parallel to another description.

book:web_81316980.description: Ethnographic study of the Ainu people of Japan, originally published in 1881. The author is often cited as 'Scheube' in older references, but the actual author is Heinrich von Siebold; 'Scheube' may be a misattribution or a different work.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Scheube's book as a source for information about the Ainos.

book:web_59c015c2.description: Geographic and ethnographic description of Kamchatka, first published in Russian in 1755; also known in German as 'Kamtschatka'.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Kraschennikow's work on Kamchatka.

book:web_461070c4.description: A book describing Hindu customs and society, written by Shib Chunder Bose and published in Calcutta in 1881.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Bose's book on Hindu customs.

book:web_8fe7e919.description: An ethnographic work by British colonial administrator Thomas Herbert Lewin, describing the tribes of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and surrounding regions, first published in 1870.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a page from Lewin's book on wild tribes of south-eastern India.

book:web_f58bd80c.description: A travel and ethnographic account of the Malay Archipelago by German naturalist and explorer Hermann von Rosenberg, published in 1878.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites a page from Rosenberg's book on the Malay Archipelago.

book:web_03d1e038.description: A lost epic poem by Aristeas of Proconnesus, describing his journey to the Issedones and the legendary peoples beyond, including the one-eyed Arimaspians and gold-guarding griffins.
commentaries: Herodotus cites Aristeas's poems (the Arimaspeia) as a source of geographical claims about the lands beyond Scythia, noting that Aristeas's account differs from the report of the Scythians.

book:web_7c2bd2e4.description: A lost epic poem by Aristeas of Proconnesus describing his travels among the Issedones and other northern peoples, frequently referenced by Herodotus in The Histories.
commentaries: Herodotus refers to Aristeas as the composer of verses, and proceeds to relate a story about his life and disappearance.
Herodotus mentions Aristeas again, noting that he did not claim to have traveled beyond the Issedonians, and that he relied on hearsay for accounts of lands further away.

book:web_c7aadb91.description: A theological treatise on papal supremacy, originally part of Bellarmine's larger work 'Disputationes de controversiis christianae fidei'.
commentaries: Thomas Hobbes references Cardinal Bellarmine's work as the primary defense of the Pope's universal power, which he then proceeds to examine and refute.

book:web_a24c810e.description: A seminal legal treatise by Sir Edward Coke, first published in 1628, commenting on Thomas Littleton's 'Tenures' and a foundational text of English common law.
commentaries: Thomas Hobbes references Sir Edward Coke's commentary on Littleton to criticize the notion of an artificial perfection of reason gained through long study.
Thomas Hobbes references a legal principle from Coke's Commentaries on Litleton to illustrate a point about justice and inheritance.

book:web_c50483e2.description: A theological treatise on divine concurrence, motion, and help by the Spanish Jesuit philosopher Francisco Suárez.
commentaries: Thomas Hobbes cites a specific book by Suarez as an example of meaningless or absurd philosophical writing, pointing to its title as incomprehensible when translated.

book:web_772539f4.description: A foundational legal textbook commissioned by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I, part of the Corpus Juris Civilis, outlining the principles of Roman law.
commentaries: Thomas Hobbes references Justinian's Institutions as a source for a classification of civil laws.

book:420330.description: This edition includes, in addition to the most pertinent sections of The Fable's two volumes, a selection from Mandeville's An Enquiry into the Origin of Honor and selections from two of Mandeville's most important sources: Pierre Bayle and the Jansenist Pierre Nicole. Hundert's Introduction places Mandeville in a number of eighteenth-century debates--particularly that of the nature and morality of commercial modernity--and underscores the degree to which his work stood as a central problem, not only for hi...
commentaries: Voltaire references Mandeville's book 'Fable of the Bees' and his argument that envy is a useful passion.

book:7015458.description: This is an EXACT reproduction of a book published before 1923. This IS NOT an OCR'd book with strange characters, introduced typographical errors, and jumbled words. This book may have occasional imperfections such as missing or blurred pages, poor pictures, errant marks, etc. that were either part of the original artifact, or were introduced by the scanning process. We believe this work is culturally important, and despite the imperfections, have elected to bring it back into print as part of our continuin...
commentaries: David Hume cites Bayle's dictionary as a source for the article on Spinoza.

book:web_e5eca651.description: A philosophical work by Pierre Bayle, originally published in 1705 as a sequel to his earlier 'Divers Thoughts on the Comet'.
commentaries: Voltaire directs the reader to Bayle's work as a source for further argumentation.

book:web_c58a6c3f.description: A multi-volume history of ancient civilizations, originally published in Paris between 1730 and 1738.
commentaries: David Hume cites Rollin's admiration for a passage of ancient history, quoting Rollin's commentary on the Athenians' rejection of Themistocles' proposal.

book:web_14c2dd4b.description: A philosophical dialogue exploring themes of unity, identity, and the moral sense, later included in Shaftesbury's 'Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times'.
commentaries: David Hume cites Shaftesbury's work as an example of how a great genius can be influenced by the principles of the imagination regarding identity.

book:web_23ac9a34.description: A poem by Matthew Prior, first published in 1718, reflecting on the vanity of human pursuits, often paired with his lighter poem 'Alma' in later editions.
commentaries: David Hume cites Prior's poem 'Solomon' as an example of a serious work that, despite being paired with a humorous one in the same volume, does not cause difficulty for the reader because the two performances are considered entirely different.

book:web_ae49baed.description: A mock-heroic poem by Matthew Prior, first published in 1718, often paired with his poem 'Solomon' in later editions.
commentaries: David Hume cites Prior's poem 'Alma' as an example of a work that, despite being humorous, can be successfully paired with a serious work in the same volume because they are considered as entirely different performances.

book:web_03a32608.description: A philosophical treatise arguing that morality is based on the conformity of actions to truth, published in London.
commentaries: David Hume cites Wollaston's book as the source of the hypothesis that falsehood is the foundation of all guilt and moral deformity, and proceeds to argue against it.

book:web_8159a72f.description: A lost work by the Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician Archytas of Tarentum, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: The subject wrote three books on the philosophy of Archytas.

book:web_962c39fb.description: A lost work by Sotion of Alexandria (fl. c. 200–170 BCE) that traced the lineages and teachings of Greek philosophers, frequently cited by later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Sotion's work 'Succession of Philosophers' as a source for the same claim about barbarian wise men.

book:web_dee261e2.description: A work by the Greek doxographer Sotion, cataloguing the successions of philosophers from Thales to the Hellenistic period. It was used as a source by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Sotion's account of Aristippus living with Lais.
Diogenes Laertius cites Sotion’s book as the source for the claim that Heraclides was a pupil of Aristotle.

book:web_6a026d9c.description: Lost treatise by Eratosthenes cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Eratosthenes' treatise on Riches and Poverty for the anecdote about Pyrrho living with his sister.

book:web_5b67205a.description: Also known as Chronographiae, a multi-volume historical work covering world events from the Trojan War to the author's time, cited by later writers such as Phavorinus.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Eratosthenes' work as a source for the claim that Pythagoras was the first scientific boxer.

book:web_4be0856e.description: Lost treatise on wealth (Peri Ploutou) by the Hellenistic scholar Eratosthenes, referenced by Plutarch in Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch cites Eratosthenes' treatise 'On Riches' for the detail that a woman of Eretria helped Themistocles gain an audience with Artabanus.

book:web_1e6288bb.description: A philosophical treatise by the grammarian Seleucus of Alexandria, likely dating to the 2nd century BC. The work is lost and known only through fragments, particularly in Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Seleucus as the source for the statement that another Plato (of Rhodes) was a disciple of Panætius.

book:web_4d4e0ac7.description: A lost work on natural history and traditions, cited by Diogenes Laertius in the 3rd century AD.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Alexander the Myndian agrees with Eleusis on the same point.

book:web_358ded61.description: A lost treatise on natural philosophy by the Peripatetic philosopher Boethus of Sidon, likely written in the 2nd century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Boethus's treatise on Nature for another definition of the substance of God.

book:web_2d27248f.description: Stoic philosopher from Sidon, author of a multi-volume work 'On Fate' cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Boethus's treatise on Fate to support the doctrine that all things are produced by fate.

book:web_897a9b16.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek sceptic philosopher Theodosius, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Exact date unknown, but must predate 230 CE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Theodosius's work arguing against the label 'sceptical' for the Pyrrhonean school.

book:web_8eb2eff8.description: Lost work on the lives of philosophers, a source for Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diocles' work 'Lives of the Philosophers' as a source for Xenophon's sons' education.
Diogenes Laertius cites Diocles as the source of a story about Aristippus and Dionysius, referencing his book on the Lives of the Philosophers.

book:web_f8ee954c.description: A lost work on the lives of philosophers by Diocles of Magnesia, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diocles as a source for the information that Pyrrho was the son of Pleistarchus.

book:web_44a600b1.description: A multi-volume Stoic philosophical treatise on ethical goods, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's work on Goods to support the Stoic claim that the beautiful is the only good.
Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's treatise on the Chief Good, seventh book, for the classification of goods.
Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's treatise on Goods, nineteenth book, to deny that pleasure is a good.
Diogenes Laertius references Hecaton's second book on Goods in support of virtue's sufficiency for happiness.

book:web_a0e3693b.description: A lost work by the ancient Pyrrhonist philosopher Ænesidemus, originally composed around the 1st century BCE, expounding the skeptical philosophy of Pyrrho.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Ænesidemus's work 'Pyrrhonean Discourses' to describe Pyrrho's non-dogmatic method.
Diogenes Laertius notes that Ænesidemus wrote eight books of Pyrrhonean discourses, and situates him within the Sceptic succession.

book:web_ef5cfd42.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Apollophanes, likely composed in the 3rd century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollophanes in his Natural Philosophy regarding the vacuum.

book:web_35614104.description: A lost treatise on painting by the ancient Greek painter Melanthius of Sicyon, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Melanthius was a prominent artist and writer on art in the 4th century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Melanthius's treatise on Painting to support a description of Polemo's character.

book:17910056.description:
The fourth and final book in the Shadow Grail series by the "New York Times "and "USA Today "bestselling authors Mercedes Lackey and Rosemary Edghill
Spirit White and her friends Burke, Loch, and Addie have escaped from Oakhurst Academy. But their freedom has come at a terrible cost--a dear friend sacrificed her own life to save theirs. In the wake of Muirin's death, they are also forced to deal with the terrifying truth behind the facade of Oakhurst Academy: all of the legends are true.
Queen Guinevere, Ki...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Ion's work 'Victories' as evidence that Pythagoras wrote poems attributed to Orpheus.

book:web_a2ae528c.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Persaeus of Citium, containing anecdotes and discussions from symposia, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Persaeus's work 'Convivial Reminiscences' as the source for Zeno refusing supper invitations.

book:web_becc877f.description: A lost ethical treatise by the Stoic philosopher Persaeus, student of Zeno of Citium, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Persaeus's work Ethical School for Zeno's age at death and arrival in Athens.

book:web_ac832144.description: A lost biographical work by Hermippus of Smyrna, a Peripatetic philosopher of the 3rd century BCE, known for his collections of lives of famous men.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hermippus' 'Lives' for an anecdote attributing to Thales a saying about thanking fortune.

book:web_154ff229.description: A lost work by the Greek rhetorician Alcimus, addressed to Amyntas (possibly a Macedonian king). Cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 AD).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Alcimus's essays to show Plato's use of Epicharmus' ideas.

book:web_a85728b3.description: An epitome or abridgment by Heraclides Lembus of the biographical work of Satyrus of Callatis, now lost.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides's abridgment of Satyrus for the account of Zeno's arrest and death.

book:web_b6733ae6.description: A lost epitome by Heraclides Lembus summarizing Sotion's work on the successions of philosophers, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius provides an anecdote about Demetrius’s advice to Ptolemy, sourced from Heraclides’s epitome.

book:web_33c13d9d.description: Historical work by Theopompus covering the reign of Philip II of Macedon, also known as the Philippica.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Theopompus's work to report the Magi's beliefs about resurrection and immortality.

book:web_058b07d9.description: A collection of marvels and strange tales by the Greek historian Theopompus, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Theopompus's 'Strange Stories' for a story about Epimenides building a temple.

book:web_a13ad409.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher and historian Phavorinus (c. 80–160 AD), cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus's Commentaries and Demetrius's essay for the existence of another Pittacus the lawgiver.
Diogenes Laertius references Phavorinus' Commentaries to mention Socrates' visit to the Isthmus.
Diogenes Laertius references Phavorinus' work 'Commentaries' for a chronological detail about Plato's death.
Diogenes Laertius references Phavorinus' 'Commentaries' to support a statement about the origin of dialogue form.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus's work 'Commentaries' as the source for a saying.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus's work to support a claim about Demetrius's lineage.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus' 'Commentaries' for the claim that Pythagoras was the first to train athletes on meat.
Diogenes Laertius mentions finding an anecdote about Empedocles in Phavorinus' Commentaries.
Phavorinus is cited as the source for the anecdote about Apis licking Eudoxus' garment.

book:web_b792e3b0.description: A lost historical work by the Greek philosopher and historian Phavorinus of Arelate, written in the early 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus' work as evidence that Anaximander placed gnomons on sun-dials in Lacedaemon.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus' Universal History to claim Socrates was the first to teach oratory.
Diogenes Laertius references Phavorinus's work to support the claim that Plato was born in Aegina.
Diogenes Laertius references Phavorinus's work to note that Plato's Republic can be found almost entire in the Contradictions of Protagoras.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus as a source for the detail about Bion following Antigonus in a litter.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus as a source for an anecdote about Carneades.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus as a source for the identity of Aristotle's prosecutor.
Diogenes Laertius credits Phavorinus with the claim about Aristotle's pioneering courtroom speech.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus twice in this passage as the source for the claim that the Athenians acted under the king’s orders and that Demetrius was impeached for illegality.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus' 'Universal History' as the source for a story involving Aristippus.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Phavorinus' Universal History as a source for the claim that certain tragedies were written after Diogenes' death.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus' 'Universal History' for the earlier diet of athletes before Pythagoras.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus as a source for the claim that Alcmæon first wrote a treatise on natural philosophy.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus as the source for the claim that Parmenides was the first to use the 'Achilles' argument.
Diogenes Laertius cites Phavorinus's work as a source for Democritus's criticism of Anaxagoras.

book:web_02452518.description: A lost work on the successions of philosophers, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Sosicrates's book 'Successions' as a source for a detail about Diodorus of Aspendos.
Diogenes Laertius cites Sosicrates as asserting that the books attributed to Diogenes are not genuine.
Diogenes Laertius cites Sosicrates' work 'Successions' for an anecdote about Pythagoras coining the term 'philosopher'.

book:web_1bf42860.description: Ancient lost work by Hippobotus, a Greek doxographer, listing and describing various philosophers, known through citations in later works such as Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hippobotus' 'Description of the Philosophers' for a list of the seven sages.

book:web_14b62f82.description: A lost doxographical work by the ancient Greek philosopher Hippobotus, cataloging and describing the various philosophical sects. It is cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hippobotus's Treatise on Sects as a source for the Cyrenaic view that pleasure is good regardless of its cause.

book:web_a9724a7d.description: An epitome or summary of the lost work 'Succession of Philosophers' by Sotion of Alexandria, compiled by Heraclides (likely Heraclides Lembus, a 2nd-century BC Greek philosopher and historian). The original Sotion work dates to around 200–170 BC, and Heraclides' abridgment was produced in the 2nd century BC, well before 230 AD.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' work 'Abridgment of Sotion' as a source listing poems attributed to Pythagoras.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Heraclides's 'Abridgment of Sotion' as a source claiming Epicurus was raised in Samos.

book:web_97e10f6b.description: A lost work by Heraclides of Pontus, an ancient Greek philosopher and writer (c. 390–310 BCE), likely summarizing earlier philosophical or historical material.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' Abridgment for a detail about an Olympic victory.

book:web_35232287.description: A collection of sayings and anecdotes by the Stoic philosopher Hecaton of Rhodes, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's collection of sayings for one of Antisthenes' aphorisms.
Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's work Apophthegms as a source for Zeno's behavior at dinner parties.

book:web_d76884e6.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Hecaton of Rhodes, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Hecaton's treatise on the Passions as a source for the classification of perturbations.

book:web_eb38346c.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Hecaton of Rhodes, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Hecaton was a student of Panaetius and active in the 2nd–1st century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's first book on Virtues for a classification of virtues.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Hecaton's third book on Virtues in the context of virtues following one another.

book:web_ef1c317f.description: A treatise by the Stoic philosopher Hecaton, quoted by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Hecaton wrote at least 13 books on the subject.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hecaton's similar statement about the wise man praying.

book:web_0e4243b4.description: Lost treatise on mathematics by Hermodorus, a Platonic philosopher from Syracuse, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Hermodorus's treatise 'On Mathematics' for a calculation concerning the time from the Magi to the fall of Troy.

book:web_67a7f825.description: A lost work by the grammarian and philosopher Thrasyllus (1st century AD), serving as an introduction or prolegomena to the writings of Democritus. It is referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Thrasylus's work 'the Events' for an alternate dating of Democritus's birth relative to Socrates.

book:web_5df805e9.description: A work by the Pyrrhonist philosopher Aenesidemus, likely written in the 1st century BCE, outlining the skeptical method of comparing appearances to reveal contradiction and confusion.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Ænesidemus's work to define the Pyrrhonean system.

book:web_e85d4f63.description: A lost work on Stoic dialectic by the Stoic philosopher Crinis, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Crinis's 'Dialectic Art' to define the adjunctive proposition.

book:web_aa5ba5ab.description: A collection of miscellaneous notes by the Peripatetic philosopher Hieronymus of Rhodes, now lost but known from fragments and citations in later works.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hieronymus of Rhodes as a source for an anecdote about Thales making money from an olive crop.

book:web_cd461041.description: A lost treatise by Demetrius of Magnesia (1st century BCE) discussing poets and prose writers who share the same name, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius of Magnesia's treatise to argue that a letter attributed to Epimenides is a modern forgery.

book:web_cb47bb06.description: Work by Demetrius of Magnesia listing individuals with the same name, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius of Magnesia's treatise for a list of other men named Thales.
Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius to assert that Hippasus left no writings.
Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius's work for an alternative version of Zeno's attack on the tyrant.

book:web_774cd752.description: A lost work by Demetrius of Magnesia (1st century BCE) listing and distinguishing famous individuals who shared the same name, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius the Magnesian's essay as a source for the anecdote about Zeno's cloak being blown off.
Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius of Magnesia's treatise as a source for the account of Heraclides delivering his country from tyrants.
Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius's work for a detail about Chrysippus's personal life.
Diogenes Laertius references Demetrius's book as evidence for Democritus's travels to Egypt.

book:web_06cafff8.description: A lost work by Demetrius of Magnesia (1st century BCE) cataloguing individuals who shared the same name, cited by Plutarch in his Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch references Demetrius of Magnesia's book 'On Persons of the Same Name' as a source for the detail about Demosthenes' wife.

book:web_84441cc0.description: A lost work by the grammarian Myronianus of Alexandria, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 AD). The work likely contained anecdotes and comparisons about philosophers and historical figures.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Myronianus' work 'Resemblances' for a tradition about Plato's death.

book:web_c09439c0.description: A lost work by Myronianus of Amastra, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 CE). The work likely contained historical anecdotes about philosophers. No surviving copies are known, and the exact date of composition is uncertain but before 230 CE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Myronianus's work 'Similar Historical Chapters' as the source for the story about Theophrastus's slave Pomphylus.

book:web_965aa4a8.description: A lost work by the Greek grammarian Myronianus, containing comparisons (similitudes) often cited by later authors like Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Myronianus's work 'Similitudes' as a source for the anecdote about Xenocrates refusing money from Antipater.

book:web_231e78e0.description: Lost work on lawgivers by Apollodorus of Athens, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's work for the fact that Solon first assembled the nine archons to deliver opinions.

book:web_c0e9d16c.description: A lost work by the Greek grammarian and historian Apollodorus of Athens (c. 180–120 BCE), likely a compilation of philosophical doctrines. The citation in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 CE) refers to this work, which existed before 230 CE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Apollodorus's work to contrast the writings of Epicurus and Chrysippus, claiming that Chrysippus's books are largely composed of quotations from other authors.

book:web_49c43487.description: A chronicle of Greek history and mythology, originally composed in verse, covering events from the Fall of Troy to the 2nd century BC.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus' 'Chronicles' for the dating of Thales' birth and death.
Diogenes Laertius refers to Apollodorus's Chronicles for an alternative account of the district dispute.
Diogenes Laertius references Apollodorus's 'Chronicles' for the birth date of Euripides.
Diogenes Laertius uses Apollodorus's Chronicles to establish the date of Plato's birth.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus' 'Chronicles' for information about the writings Crates left behind.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus for the date of Carneades' death.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus as a source for Aristotle's birth date and chronology.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's Chronicles for the date of Chrysippus's death.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's 'Chronicles' for the age of Gorgias.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's Chronicles for information about Zeno's parentage.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's Chronicles as providing the birth date of Democritus.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus as a source for the claim that Pyrrho was originally a painter.

book:web_4343a08d.description: A work by Damon of Cyrene that critiques philosophers, with particular focus on the Seven Sages. It is cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Damon the Cyrenæan as a writer who reproached the seven sages.

book:web_4a4bf8b1.description: A lost biographical work by Antigonus of Carystus, a 3rd-century BCE Greek writer, known for its anecdotes about philosophers and cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antigonus's 'Lives' as a source for details about Polemo's family background.

book:web_bdc4a10a.description: A lost comedy by the Athenian playwright Cratinus, likely satirizing or referencing the poets Homer and Hesiod, as mentioned in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Cratinus's work to show that poets were called Sophists.

book:web_52f5548e.description: A lost comedy by the Greek playwright Mnesimachus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Mnesimachus' play 'Alcmæon' as a comedic reference to Pythagorean dietary practices.

book:web_42a5b07c.description: A lost work by the Cyrenaic philosopher Theodorus of Cyrene (the Atheist), attacking various philosophical schools. Mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Theodorus's attack on Aristippus in his Treatise on Sects.

book:web_6d8af158.description: A lost historical work by the Athenian author Stesiclides, listing archons and Olympic victors. The text is known only from fragments and citations in later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius (Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, c. 230 CE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Stesiclides' work 'List of Archons and Conquerors at Olympia' for the date of Xenophon's death.

book:web_069a5e3c.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Antipater of Tarsus, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, discussing the nature of the cosmos.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater's treatise on the World to present a different view on the substance of God.

book:web_73d1d61a.description: A lost Stoic philosophical treatise by Antipater of Tarsus, head of the Stoic school, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater's treatise on Substance to state that body is a substance and finite.

book:web_c73ed118.description: A lost treatise on definitions by the Stoic philosopher Antipater of Tarsus, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in his 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers'.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater's first book 'On Definitions' for his definition of definition.

book:web_d50441c8.description: Lost work on animals by the Stoic philosopher Antipater of Tarsus, mentioned by the Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Antipater of Tarsus's work 'History of Animals' as mentioned by a scholiast.

book:web_67412370.description: Lost work by Hermippus of Smyrna, a 3rd-century BCE biographer, recounting the sale of the philosopher Diogenes into slavery.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hermippus' 'Sale of Diogenes' as a source for the story of Diogenes' captivity and sale.

book:web_d14effdb.description: A work by Hermippus of Smyrna describing the sayings and deeds of the Seven Wise Men of ancient Greece, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Hermippus for the fact that Eudoxus gave laws to his city.

book:web_b2237340.description: A lost work by the Academic skeptic philosopher Clitomachus, discussing various philosophical sects.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Clitomachus's Essay on Sects as a source for the Cyrenaic rejection of natural philosophy and dialectics.

book:web_3c96821d.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Athenodorus (possibly Athenodorus Cordylion or Athenodorus Cananites), cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The work likely contained biographical and doxographical material on earlier philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Athenodorus's work 'Philosophical Conversations' as the source for Theophrastus's parentage and occupation.
Diogenes Laertius cites Theodorus's work for an anecdote about Plato serving as choregus.

book:web_ef488ec6.description: A lost work by Athenodorus, likely the Stoic philosopher Athenodorus Cordylion (or Athenodorus of Tarsus), cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The work is known only through fragments.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Athenodorus's Conversations as a source for Diogenes's shining appearance.
Diogenes Laertius cites Athenodorus's 'Conversations' for an anecdote about Democritus and Hippocrates.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's work on the Gods to support Zeno's view on the substance of God.

book:33281256.description:
On Love is a collection of short stories and prose poems designed to capture, in quick staccato sentences and descriptions that blossom in complexity and content, the essence of love.
These depictions of romance are diverse creations that reflect more than infatuation: they also examine connections and distance, the ebb and flow of attraction, the sadness of separation, and the angst of evolution and change.
Each of the six pieces contains a sense of heartfelt relationships juxtaposed by loneliness; the ach...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius attributes the view that love is a part of friendship to Chrysippus's essay On Love.

book:web_2cceaa38.description: A lost work by Hecataeus of Abdera (c. 360–290 BCE), a Greek historian and philosopher. It was likely part of his 'Aegyptiaca', an ethnographic and historical study of Egypt that included accounts of Egyptian philosophy and religion.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Hecatæus's work to confirm Manetho's account of Egyptian philosophy.

book:web_c4674f5b.description: A lost Stoic philosophical work on the elements, likely by Archedemus of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher active in the 2nd century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Archedemus in a treatise on the Elements discussing the same topic.

book:web_36a43e24.description: A lost philosophical work on the Stoic theory of elements, attributed to the Stoic philosopher Archedemus of Tarsus (fl. c. 140 BC).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Archedemus's work On Elements for the same principles.

book:web_3e491ab6.description: A work by the Stoic philosopher Archedemus of Tarsus, referenced by Diogenes Laertius. The exact date is uncertain, but Archedemus flourished in the 2nd century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Archedemus's 'On the Voice' for the claim that voice is a body.

book:web_318c0fed.description: A lost work by Andron, likely a historical or philosophical treatise, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The title refers to the tripod offered as a prize for wisdom.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Andron's book 'The Tripod' for a version involving Argives and Aristodemus.

book:web_fb948de7.description: A treatise by the Stoic philosopher Antipater of Tarsus, discussing semantics and qualities.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater's treatise for an additional quality to the parts of a sentence.

book:web_0ee50e6a.description: A play by the Athenian dramatist Menander, a representative of New Comedy, likely written in the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE. Only fragments survive.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies a line as from Menander's Citharista.

book:web_32de79bc.description: Greek philosopher and historian, student of Epicurus, wrote about Socrates and the Socratic school.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Idomeneus as a source confirming Socrates' rhetorical skill.
Diogenes Laertius references Idomeneus' essay on the Socratic School to support the claim about Socrates teaching oratory.
Diogenes Laertius cites Idomeneus as an authority for an alternative account of a Platonic dialogue's attribution.
Diogenes Laertius cites Idomeneus as a source for an alternative attribution of a speech in Plato's Crito.

book:web_92b5a24a.description: Lost work on philosophical sects by the Stoic philosopher Panætius of Rhodes.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Panætius's book on Sects as a source for the Cyrenaic doctrine that bodily pleasure is the chief good.

book:web_aef9dd33.description: A lost work by Demetrius of Phalerum (or possibly another Demetrius), cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The essay discussed individuals sharing the same name, such as Pittacus.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Demetrius's essay that mentions the other Pittacus.

book:15744291.description: Secrets, lies and coincidences abound in this story of a young girl looking for her father. Alice, now twenty-one years old, is determined to find her father who left home when she was just a baby, despite a warning from her mother that she should not look for him. Her mother's secretiveness over the subject is because of the guilt she feels about keeping the truth from Alice. It will take all of Alice's courage to persevere in her search. There are doubts and uncertainties at every turn. Coincidences is a....
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Mysonianus's 'Coincidences' for the claim that Cretans call Epimenides one of the Curetes.

book:web_9b483f0f.description: Lost work on ethics by the Peripatetic philosopher Eudromus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in his 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers' (c. 230). Exact date unknown, but existed before 230.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Eudromus also used this division in his work 'Ethical Elements'.

book:web_1b46b738.description: A lost work by the Peripatetic philosopher Phanias of Eresus (4th–3rd century BCE), cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Phanias was a student of Aristotle and a contemporary of Theophrastus.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Phanias's treatise as the source for a Socratic-style exchange with Antisthenes.

book:web_c5e8fdaa.description: A lost work by the otherwise unknown author Sabinus, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (3rd century CE) as a source for the philosopher Mnesistratus of Thasos. No surviving copies or precise dating exist, but it must have been written before 230 CE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Sabinus' work 'Meditative Matter' for adding a name to the list of Plato's disciples.

book:web_56ba7b42.description: A lost historical work by Euphantus of Olynthus, a philosopher of the Megarian school, covering events of his own time (c. 4th–3rd century BCE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Euphantus as a source for an account of Menedemus's embassy to Demetrius regarding Oropus.

book:web_cf96cb3d.description: A lost work of commentary on the satirical poems (Silli) of Timon of Phlius, written by the Stoic philosopher Apollonides of Nicaea and dedicated to Tiberius Caesar.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Apollonides's first book of 'Commentaries on the Silli' as a source for biographical details about Timon.

book:29388402.description:
"I glared up at my father's house, my unhappy childhood home. I'd sworn that I'd never come back..."
Seven years ago, Kasey Clayton left her unhappy hometown of Roseburg, Oregon. Since then, everything's gone downhill. Her apartment's tiny, her job sucks, her car's a rolling bucket of rust, and she hasn't been on a date in months.And now, her father has died - but he's left his dilapidated house in Roseburg to her.
This could be Kasey's chance. If she can clean up, repair, and sell her father's house, she'l...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's first book on Duty for the same view about justice and animals.

book:web_cd974e0c.description: A play by the ancient Greek comic poet Sophilus, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Stilpo was ridiculed by Sophilus in his play.

book:web_7d8088bb.description: Lost ancient biography of Dion of Syracuse, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Author Timocrates is a Greek historian or biographer, likely active in the 4th century BC.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Timocrates's 'Life of Dion' for the duration of Zeno's studies under Stilpon and Xenocrates.

book:web_d3d1dcfe.description: A lost satirical work by Diogenes the Cynic, mentioned in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Diogenes' own book 'Pordalus' where he confesses to adulterating the coinage.

book:web_75fd8812.description: A lost work on Stoic ethics by Apollodorus of Seleucia, a Stoic philosopher of the 2nd century BC, cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Apollodorus, in his Ethics, follows Hecaton's classification of goods.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's definition of grief as an irrational contraction of the soul.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus calling Cynicism a short path to virtue.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's Ethics for the doctrine about the wise man loving those with natural aptitude for virtue.

book:web_6858778f.description: A work by Duris of Samos, likely a geographical or historical treatise, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Duris' work as the source for an epigram about Pherecydes.

book:web_53706099.description: A lost philosophical work by the eclectic Platonist Potamo of Alexandria, active around the 1st century BCE. The text discussed criteria of truth, as referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Potamo's 'Elementary Instruction' to explain his criteria of truth and foundational principles for the Eclectic school.

book:web_f396dd57.description: A lost work by Demetrius of Troezen, quoted by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 AD). The exact date of composition is unknown but it existed before 230 AD.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius' book where he reports a quotation from Homer about suicide.

book:web_d5242f80.description: A historical work by the Sicilian Greek historian Timaeus, covering the history of Sicily and Magna Graecia, now lost except for fragments.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Timaeus' 'Histories' for Pythagoras' statements about the names of married women.

book:web_2e88f7fd.description: A lost treatise on linguistic theory by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Babylon, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diogenes' treatise 'On Voice' as the source for the classification of sentence parts.

book:web_b2df9ec9.description: A lost work on dialectic by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Babylon, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diogenes's 'Dialectic Art' as another source for the definition of the combined proposition.

book:web_0fedf580.description: Cynic philosopher and poet, known for his work Treatise on Opinions (Περὶ δοξῶν) and compilation of the Greek Anthology.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Meleager's Treatise on Opinions as a source for the Cyrenaic rejection of natural philosophy and dialectics.

book:web_209d80d6.description: A historical work on Persia by the Greek historian Deinon (also known as Dinon), written in the 4th century BCE. It is cited by later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius and Plutarch.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Deinon's History of Persia to corroborate the parentage of Protagoras.

book:web_40eb0016.description: Epicurean philosophical work by Diogenes the Epicurean (likely Diogenes of Oenoanda), referred to by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diogenes the Epicurean as asserting a similar doctrine about eclipses in his 'Select Opinions'.
Diogenes is mentioned as a contemporary philosopher who engaged in witty exchanges with the subject.
Diogenes Laertius refers to Diogenes' letters as a source for his use of a cask as a house.
Diogenes Laertius attributes the philosophical teachings and arguments to Diogenes of Sinope, citing him as the source of these ideas.
Diogenes Laertius lists Diogenes the Babylonian as one who followed the division.
Diogenes Laertius attributes to Diogenes a definition of the chief good as acting according to sound reason.
The excerpt identifies Monimus as a pupil of Diogenes, referencing Diogenes as a source of his ideas.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's second book of his Natural Philosophy for the theory of vision involving a cone of air.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's second book of his Natural Philosophy defining seed as a spirit according to substance.

book:22006285.description:
J2 Fanfic
Jared is a makeup artist and is hired for a new movie based in Vancouver. Jensen plays the part of a hardcore, punk-rock star, but he has a real-life attitude problem. Unfortunately, Jared can't figure out why and he still finds Jensen attractive. They have to work alone together; long hours and long days, in small quarters of the makeup trailer. During that time, Jared discovers the actor's secret and wants nothing more than to break away the protective mask Jensen hides behind.
Art by tinkabell0...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Thespis as the one who introduced the first actor into tragedy.

book:web_6476ff00.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek historian Dieuchidas of Megara, likely written in the 4th century BCE, known only from fragmentary references in later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Dieuchidas's work to support the claim that Solon, not Pisistratus, brought Homer to light.

book:web_2e4466e7.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Ariston of Chios, cited by Diogenes Laërtius, providing an account of the life and death of Heraclitus.
commentaries: Ariston is cited in his work about Heraclitus for an alternative account of his death.

book:web_17587061.description: Work by Phlegon of Tralles (2nd century AD) cataloging individuals who lived exceptionally long lives, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Phlegon's book on long-lived people as a source for Epimenides' age at death.

book:web_e62e8403.description: A lost Stoic philosophical treatise in at least ten books, cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater of Tyre in the eighth book of his treatise On the World asserting the aether as the dominant principle.
Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater in his essay On the World also asserting the world is spherical.
Diogenes Laertius cites Antipater in the tenth book of his treatise On the World discussing creation and destruction.

book:18453708.description:
Dear Author,
He used to be a damn good agent until he threw it all away. He's been on the run for two years, but we finally pinned down his location. They sent me to bring him in. I've got him, but he's fighting me every step of the way. He won't go in willingly, and I won't go without him. Oh, and I'd really like a gun fight between them at some point...
Photo Description:
Two naked men lie facedown on a flat rock, the man on top has his left arm on top of the lower man's head. The lower man has both hands...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Chrysippus's first book on Justice for the claim that no obligations of justice bind us to animals.

book:703752.description: Kurt Busiek and Alex Ross' fully-painted re-telling of key moments in the Marvel Universe (as seen through the eyes of an innocent bystander) is presented in this collected edition.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Theopompus as the source for the claim that Pherecydes told the Lacedaemonians to honour neither gold nor silver.

book:34469954.description:
I got a 12 inch python and I'm gonna hide it in your bush...
There's not a woman alive able to tame me. You won't be the first to try. You won't be the last to fail.
You simply won't get past my 8-pack abs, rugged face, and ripped body.
Let's not forget the name of this book.
Once you see my python twitch, your mouth will go dry.
It'll get thicker and you'll want to touch it.
It'll change it's color and you'll want to taste it.
And once you do...
My venom will shoot inside of you.
And make you wild.
That's....
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Python as a source for Timon's verse about Pyrrho.
Diogenes Laertius references Timon's work 'Python' to support the claim that Pyrrho does not undermine custom.

book:web_385d4abd.description: A lost Hellenistic historical work by Ister (or Istros), a pupil of Callimachus, covering Attic mythology and antiquities. The citation refers to its thirteenth book, which contained an account of Aethra.

book:web_2d360b44.description: A Latin grammarian and author of the encyclopedic work 'De Compendiosa Doctrina' which preserves many fragments of earlier Latin authors.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Nonius Marcellus's quotation of Varro on the fish's name.

book:web_6a822206.description: A work by the Greek historian and physician Ctesias, describing India and its wonders, written around the 5th century BCE.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Pliny likely derived his description of the crocotta from Ctesias's work.

book:15925337.description: Although written over four hundred years after Alexander's death, Arrian's 'Campaigns of Alexander' is our best source of knowledge of the man and his deeds. Arrain had himself been a military commander, and his record of the exploits of the world's greatest conqueror reveals sympathy for his subject, without the adulation or contempt which so often mar other histories of the time. Arrain's unaffected style of writing, with its matter-of-fact tone, offsets the remarkable career and paradoxical nature of Ale...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Arrian quotes Megasthenes in his Indica.

book:web_06b5a987.description: A military treatise by Arrian (Lucius Flavius Arrianus), written around 136 AD, describing cavalry tactics and equipment, including light cavalry types such as Tarentines and horse archers.
commentaries: Polybius cites Arrian's Tactica to distinguish types of cavalry.

book:web_dfdfce3b.description: A biography of the Roman emperor Elagabalus (Heliogabalus), part of the Historia Augusta, a late Roman collection of imperial biographies traditionally attributed to six authors including Lampridius, though the work's actual date and authorship are debated.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Lampridius as a source for the restoration of the euripus to the Circus.

book:web_8604b8c5.description: A comprehensive work on the history of magic, originally published in German as 'Geschichte der Magie' (1844), translated into English and published in Bohn's Standard Library editions.

book:web_de12bfd0.description: A two-volume work by the French Protestant theologian and scholar Samuel Bochart, first published in 1663, which systematically examines animals mentioned in the Bible, drawing on classical and natural history sources.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Bochart's work on Animals as a source for accounts of huge fishes.

book:web_18ed0ac4.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek grammarian Apion, detailing Egyptian history and culture, referenced by Aulus Gellius.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Aulus Gellius relates a story from Apion's work, with Apion claiming to have witnessed the event.

book:web_ae6872d6.description: A travelogue by British diplomat and artist Henry Salt, documenting his journey into the interior of Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia) in 1809-1810.

Reprint of the 1957 edition.

Useful maps are provided, along with Notes on the text,....

book:19511472.description: This is a new edition of The Complete Commentaries of Julius Caesar. Including The Commentaries on The War in Gaul and The Roman Civil War. book:web_5c9a05ff.description: Lost poem written by Julius Caesar in his youth, referenced in Suetonius's 'The Twelve Caesars'.
commentaries: Suetonius lists Cicero's youthful poem Glaucus Pontius and notes it was still extant in Plutarch's time.

book:web_2322ae15.description: A treatise on architecture written by the Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius, dedicated to Emperor Augustus, covering building materials, construction techniques, and the principles of design.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Vitruvius for the invention of the square by Pythagoras.

book:web_5ec61506.description: A Christian apologetic work by Tatian, written in the 2nd century, defending Christianity against Greek culture and philosophy.
commentaries: Voltaire references Tatian's 'Oratio ad Graecos' to present his view that the soul is composite.

book:web_92524699.description: A medieval encyclopedia of zoology and natural history, drawing on Aristotle and Arabic sources, written by the 13th-century scholar Albertus Magnus.

Pliny the Elder references Albertus Magnus's fuller account of the method for capturing wild elephants.

book:web_a3bf9c79.description: A series of nine homilies by Basil the Great on the six days of creation, delivered around 370 AD.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Basil's homily as attributing craftiness to the crab.

book:web_675177d9.description: Lost agricultural treatise by Hiero II of Syracuse, referenced by Roman writers Varro and Columella.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Hiero II's 'Treatise on Agriculture' as mentioned by Varro and Columella.

book:web_23c27cf1.description: A history of Sicily by the Greek historian Philistus, written in the 4th century BCE.
commentaries: Plutarch notes that Harpalus sent Philistus's History to Alexander.

book:551629.description:
Valerius Maximus compiled his handbook of notable deeds and sayings during the reign of Tiberius (14-37 CE). The collection was very popular in the Renaissance and has recently attracted renewed scholarly attention. Yet to date there has been no modern English translation of "Memorable Doings and Sayings." This work is now added to the Loeb Classical Library, a freshly edited Latin text facing D. R. Shackleton Bailey's pleasing and authoritative translation.
Valerius arranges his instructive examples in sho...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Valerius Maximus for a historical fact about the family.

book:web_4f7e470c.description: A work by Lazzaro Spallanzani on the natural history and migration of eels in the Lagoon of Comacchio, originally published in Italian as 'Storia naturale dell'anguilla della laguna di Comacchio' or in a letter form.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Spallanzani's work on the life cycle of eels.

book:web_b74a7031.description: A work on the fishes of the Ganges, originally published in 1822. The author, Francis Hamilton (formerly Buchanan), was a Scottish naturalist.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder quotes Hamilton Buchanan's work on Bengal fishes.

book:web_41dc1d74.description: A medieval treatise on falconry and ornithology, written by Emperor Frederick II. It is one of the earliest scientific works on bird behavior and hunting with birds of prey.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Frederick II's work to support a claim about the bird's name.

book:web_8ba45a03.description: A collection of remarkable and curious anecdotes, including instances of multiple births, published in the late 17th century.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Wanley's book as a source of apparently authentic instances of multiple births.

book:web_c35f8c73.description: A posthumously published work by Ulisse Aldrovandi (Latinized as Aldrovandus), a Renaissance naturalist, compiling descriptions and illustrations of mythical and real monsters, anomalies, and curiosities.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder quotes Aldrovandus's book on monsters.

book:web_8f47de38.description: English writer and skeptic who published 'The Discoverie of Witchcraft' in 1584, arguing against the belief in witches and exposing fraud.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder quotes Reginald Scott's Discovery of Witchcraft on the effect of bewitching eyes.

book:web_a7e47f9f.description: A history of the Christian church from the Arian perspective, written by Philostorgius in the 5th century, now surviving only in fragments and an epitome by Photius.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder mentions that Philostorgius tells a similar story of a martyr saved by a dolphin.

book:web_d0d0fd57.description: A lost work by Munatius Rufus, a friend of Cato the Younger, which was a primary source for later biographies of Cato, including that by Thrasea Paetus.
commentaries: Plutarch notes that Munatius wrote a book about Cato, which Thrasea later used as a main source.

book:web_f6d00c5c.description: A multi-volume history of the papacy, covering the period from the early church to the Reformation.

book:7480592.description: Gils Blas recounts the education and swashbuckling adventures of an adaptable young valet as he progresses from one master to the next, making his way from naive youth to cunning servant to landed proprietor and nobleman--with a stint in jail, bereavements, and fits of remorse along the way. commentaries: Arthur Schopenhauer cites this novel as a notable exception to the generally harmful influence of novels on youth.

book:12230469.description: This is a pre-1923 historical reproduction that was curated for quality. book:pg30755.description:
The Doctor and Charley decide to take a well-deserved break from the monotony of being chased, shot at and generally suffering anti-social behaviour at the hands of others. Which would be a momentous, if rather dispiriting, event to witness in itself. However, the machinations of a love-sick aristocrat, a proud art historian and a rabid High Priest of a really quite dodgy cult....

q: "the Divine Idea of the World, that which lies at the bottom of Appearance," as Fichte styles it

Fichte calls the Man of Letters, therefore, a Prophet, or as he prefers to phrase it, a Priest, continually unfolding the Godlike to men: Men of Letters are a perpetual Priesthood, from age to age, teaching all men that a God is still present in their life, that all "Appearance," whatsoever we see in the world, is but as a vesture for the "Divine Idea of the World," for "that which lies at the bottom of Appearance."
Fichte discriminates with sharp zeal the _true_ Literary Man, what we here call the _Hero_ as Man of Letters, from multitudes of false unheroic.

Whoever lives not wholly in this Divine Idea, or living partially in it, struggles not, as for the one good, to live wholly in it,--he is, let him live where else he like, in what pomps and prosperities he like, no Literary Man; he is, says Fichte, a "Bungler, _Stumper_."

Or at best, if he belong to the prosaic provinces, he may be a "Hodman;" Fichte even calls him elsewhere a "Nonentity," and has in short no mercy for him, no wish that _he_ should continue happy among us!
It may well enough be named, in Fichte's style, a "continuous revelation" of the Godlike in the Terrestrial and Common.

and she hastened the more eagerly to the Church, and hung upon the lips of Ambrose, praying for the fountain of that water, which springeth up unto life everlasting.
and with joy I heard Ambrose in his sermons to the people, oftentimes most diligently recommend this text for a rule, The letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life;

And by letters I signified to Thy Prelate, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and present desires, begging his advice what of Thy Scriptures I had best read, to become readier and fitter for receiving so great grace.
I remembered those true verses of Thy Ambrose.

q: Mr Hume observes, that in the Saxon times, the fleece was estimated at two-fifths of the value of the whole sheep and that this was much above the proportion of its present estimation.

Mr Hume frequently takes notice of the inability of the ancient kings of England to carry on, without interruption, any foreign war of long duration.

Adam Smith notes that Mr Hume has fully exposed the fallacy of the notion held by Locke, Lawe, and Montesquieu.
Adam Smith credits Mr Hume as the only writer to have observed the effect of commerce and manufactures on order and government.

q: In 1751 and 1752, when Mr Hume published his Political Discourses, and soon after the great multiplication of paper money in Scotland, there was a very sensible rise in the price of provisions, owing, probably, to the badness of the seasons, and not to the multiplication of paper money.

q: The state seems to have assigned the Academy to Plato, the Lyceum to Aristotle, and the Portico to Zeno of Citta, the founder of the Stoics.

q: In 1688, Mr Gregory King, whose skill in political arithmetic is so much extolled by Dr Davenant, computed the ordinary income of labourers and out-servants to be fifteen pounds a-year to a family, which he supposed to consist, one with another, of three and a half persons.

Mr Gregory King, a man famous for his knowledge in matters of this kind, estimated the average price of wheat, in years of moderate plenty, to be to the grower 3s. 6d. the bushel, or eight-and-twenty shillings the quarter.

By the 22d of Charles II. c. 13, the importation of wheat, whenever the price in the home market did not exceed 53s:4d. the quarter, was subjected to a duty of 16s. the quarter; and to a duty of 8s. whenever the price did not exceed £4.

q: of which Aristotle affords us a single instance, who made his natural philosophy completely subservient to his logic, and thus rendered it little more than useless and disputatious.

while Aristotle’s physics are mere logical terms, and he remodelled the same subject in his metaphysics under a more imposing title, and more as a realist than a nominalist.

Nor is much stress to be laid on his frequent recourse to experiment in his books on animals, his problems, and other treatises; for he had already decided, without having properly consulted experience as the basis of his decisions and axioms, and after having so decided, he drags experiment along as a captive constrained to accommodate herself to his decisions: so that he is even more to be blamed than his modern followers (of the scholastic school) who have deserted her altogether.

The Aristotelian philosophy, after destroying other systems (as the Ottomans do their brethren) by its disputatious confutations, decided upon everything, and Aristotle himself then raises up questions at will, in order to settle them; so that everything should be certain and decided, a method now in use among his successors.

With regard to the supposition that there is a general unanimity as to the philosophy of Aristotle, because the other systems of the ancients ceased and became obsolete on its promulgation, and nothing better has been since discovered; whence it appears that it is so well determined and founded, as to have united the suffrages of both ages; we will observe--1st. That the notion of other ancient systems having ceased after the publication of the works of Aristotle is false, for the works of the ancient philosophers subsisted long after that event, even to the time of Cicero, and the subsequent ages.
